title: Trump’s terrible plan to break skilled immigration
gist: Yglesias argues the H-1B program is already a fiscal and economic winner — median earnings of $130,075 and 2.6x the typical household's net federal contribution — and that Trump's $100,000 visa fee plus the attack on OPT does not fix the program's real design flaws but shrinks it, while perversely tilting what remains toward IT-outsourcing firms. His fix: allocate visas by actual salary and double or triple the cap.

themes.theme: The fiscal math favors H-1B as-is

insights.claim: The median H-1B worker earns $130,075 per year, the 91st percentile of the U.S. wage distribution, per Adam Ozimek and Sarah Eckhardt.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Anchor number for any debate about whether skilled-visa holders undercut American wages — they sit in the top decile.
insights.quote: the median H-1B worker earns $130,075 per year (the 91st percentile nationally)
insights.locator: Adam Ozimek and Sarah Eckhardt show

insights.claim: The average H-1B household makes a net federal fiscal contribution 2.6 times that of the typical American household, with additional gains to state and local governments.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Cutting skilled visas is a revenue-negative policy; fiscal forecasts that ignore immigration composition will misprice the deficit path.
insights.locator: meaning that the average H-1B household makes a net federal fiscal contribution

insights.claim: Because H-1B recipients are high earners, the standard objections to immigration — inequality effects and fiscal drag from low-wage workers — simply do not apply to this program.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: The anti-immigration economic case does not transfer to skilled visas; policy conflating the two is economically unjustified.
insights.locator: Immigration of full-time workers always generates a positive impact

insights.claim: Expanding the pre-Trump H-1B program with zero reforms and zero fixes would still be net good for the country, before counting any innovation-spillover or agglomeration benefits.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Sets a low bar: the bullish case for skilled immigration does not require believing the optimistic research literature.
insights.quote: If you took the program exactly as it existed pre-Trump, made zero reforms, fixed zero problems, and just made it bigger, that would be good.
insights.locator: Even if you don’t want to believe the most optimistic research findings

insights.claim: High-earning H-1B workers are customers for the large majority of working Americans who provide locally facing services, a domestic demand channel distinct from the tech sector itself.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Regional service economies in visa-dense metros are downstream of skilled-visa policy, not just tech payrolls.
insights.locator: This is a big win for the federal budget

themes.theme: The $100,000 fee kills the median job, not the abuse

insights.claim: A $100,000 per-visa fee does not merely eliminate the bottom 20-30 percent of current H-1B uses — it kills off the typical H-1B job, since the median recipient earns $130,075.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: This is the single clearest quantification that the fee is program shrinkage, not targeted reform; model a step-down in skilled inflows if it survives.
insights.quote: kills off not just the bottom 20-30 percent of current H-1B uses — it kills off the typical H-1B job
insights.locator: Setting that aside for a minute, the virtue of the $100,000 fee

insights.claim: The $100,000 H-1B fee was struck down in court on the grounds that a presidential proclamation cannot create a large new tax, and the administration is now attempting the same result through regulation instead.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: The policy's survival is a live legal question — the regulatory route is the one to watch for timing of any skilled-labor supply shock.
insights.locator: The fee idea was struck down in court

insights.claim: A parallel $100,000 fee on hiring foreign graduates through Optional Practical Training would end the OPT program outright, because even skilled workers in high-paying occupations do not earn high salaries in their first job.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Entry-level foreign hiring is the most fee-elastic segment; U.S. universities' international enrollment economics are directly exposed.

themes.theme: Second-order effect: the policy strengthens outsourcers

insights.claim: Killing OPT pushes H-1B further toward being a visa program for outsourcing firms like Infosys and Tata, because ordinary American companies typically hire foreign workers who already lived in the U.S. on a student visa and did OPT first — remove that pipeline and only the outsourcers' channel remains.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: The reform aimed at body shops would raise the outsourcers' share of what remains — a counterintuitive relative win for Indian IT-services firms' U.S. staffing model.
insights.quote: what’s left is a visa program for outsourcing companies
insights.locator: Worse, as Sam Peak and Jiaxin He wrote in an August policy brief

insights.claim: The $100,000 fee will also destroy much current outsourcing use of H-1B, but the combined effect is not reallocating visas to higher-value uses — it is squeezing the same balloon from multiple directions at once.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Net effect is pure volume contraction across all user types, not a quality upgrade — expect aggregate skilled inflows down regardless of composition arguments.
insights.quote: It’s just squeezing the balloon from multiple directions simultaneously.

insights.claim: American companies outside the large outsourcers prefer foreign-born hires who have already lived in the U.S., speak English, and have the soft skills that make them good colleagues — which is why the student-visa-to-OPT-to-H-1B pipeline is the normal corporate path.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Explains why domestic-graduate pipelines, not offshore recruiting, are what corporate America actually buys with skilled visas.

themes.theme: Design flaws: lottery and Wage Level

insights.claim: H-1B allocation ultimately runs on a lottery among applicants who clear eligibility thresholds, so the government is stingy with visas while being only slightly selective about who receives them.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: The scarcity is real but the selection is weak — the cheapest quality upgrade is changing allocation, not cutting volume.
insights.locator: From a policy-design standpoint, the H-1B visa program has two big design flaws

insights.claim: H-1B wage rules benchmark salary against the occupational category in a given labor market rather than against the entire U.S. wage spectrum, so they fail to select for high absolute pay.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Explains why occupation-relative wage tests do not deliver the fiscal selection policymakers think they are buying.
insights.locator: The other design flaw is that while there are a bunch of wage requirements

insights.claim: The proposed wage-weighted lottery weights by the four-part Wage Level classification rather than actual salary, producing perverse rankings: an accountant in Birmingham, Alabama earning $85,000 sits at Wage Level Three while a chemical engineer in Atlanta earning $95,000 sits at Wage Level Two.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A reform marketed as merit-weighting would in practice misallocate against the higher-paid worker — a concrete flaw to cite when the rule is litigated or scored.
insights.quote: an accountant in Birmingham, Ala., earning $85,000 would be at Wage Level Three
insights.locator: It shows that, for example, an accountant in Birmingham

insights.claim: The prescription is to double or triple the number of H-1B visas and allocate them by salary rather than by lottery, ideally implemented simultaneously.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Defines the policy state that would be maximally bullish for U.S. tech labor supply and fiscal balance — a benchmark to judge any future reform against.
insights.quote: double or triple the number of H-1B visas and allocate them by salary rather than by lottery
insights.locator: If it were up to me

insights.claim: Salary-based allocation creates a political flywheel for expansion: under it the marginal candidate who just misses out is still a very highly paid worker, making the case for raising the cap far more compelling.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Sequencing matters — allocation reform first could unlock cap expansion later, so a salary-ranking rule is the leading indicator to watch.
insights.locator: If you allocate the visas by salary

insights.claim: An automatic study-to-work pathway needs guardrails such as a minimum SAT/GRE score or salary threshold, because Boris Johnson's UK precedent shows that turning educational institutions into automatic work-visa routes incentivizes diploma mills as loopholes.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: The UK experience is the template opponents will cite; any credible U.S. graduate-retention proposal must pre-empt the diploma-mill critique.
insights.locator: The precedent from Boris Johnson’s unfortunate tenure

insights.claim: Fifteen years ago expanding skilled-worker visas was the shared goal of both parties, with the only dispute over what to pair it with; the H-1B program was relatively uncontroversial.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Shows how fast a bipartisan consensus can invert — a warning that other currently safe policy regimes can flip within a decade.
insights.locator: Fifteen years ago, the H-1B visa program

insights.claim: A large fraction of H-1B recipients staff companies whose main business is outsourcing I.T. work, usually to India, rather than helping American software companies grow — a real flaw that the backlash has overgeneralized into condemning the whole program.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: The legitimate critique is narrow and fixable; conflating it with the program's overall value is the analytical error driving the policy.

insights.claim: Trump argued publicly in August 2015 that foreigners who attend American colleges and want to stay should not be thrown out of the country, the opposite of his administration's current OPT policy.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: The president's own prior position is the rhetorical opening for graduate-retention reform, and signals the policy is not ideologically fixed.
